6. Running it in production

Say your payments rollup now runs every hour from a scheduler, while you sleep. Whatever breaks, breaks at 3 a.m.: a change merged on Friday divides by a quantity that can be zero, a batch arrives two hours late and rewrites an hour finance has already closed, or a credential ends up in a log. The rule itself is proved. What's left is the work around it. We'll check the pipeline's file before it merges, test it in CI, name its credentials without holding them, tell the next team what it guarantees through OpenLineage, and bound the state an hourly rollup keeps, with a late batch refused before it lands.

1. Check the file before it merges

A pipeline lives in a file. The sverify command proves every transform and node in it without running anything, so a CI job or a pre-commit hook can stop a change before it merges. Here is a file that computes each payment's price per unit:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
$ sverify check payments.py --diff
unit_prices: requires payments: _.qty.isnull() | (_.qty != 0)
--- a/payments.py
+++ b/payments.py
@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@
 )
 
 @sv.transform(
-    requires={"payments": [_.cents >= 0, sv.key("id")]},
+    requires={"payments": [_.cents >= 0, sv.key("id"), _.qty.isnull() | (_.qty != 0)]},
     ensures=[sv.key("id")],
 )
 def unit_prices(payments):
`sverify check --fix` writes this.
exit code 1

data.text/markdown: The key is proved, and the check found what the author missed: a payment with qty = 0 raises a division by zero, at 3 a.m., on the first such row. --diff shows the precondition that rules it out as a change to the decorator, and --fix writes it. The exit code is 1 while something is not proved, so the job fails until it is:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
$ sverify check payments.py --fix
unit_prices: requires payments: _.qty.isnull() | (_.qty != 0)
--- a/payments.py
+++ b/payments.py
@@ -10,7 +10,7 @@
 )
 
 @sv.transform(
-    requires={"payments": [_.cents >= 0, sv.key("id")]},
+    requires={"payments": [_.cents >= 0, sv.key("id"), _.qty.isnull() | (_.qty != 0)]},
     ensures=[sv.key("id")],
 )
 def unit_prices(payments):
wrote payments.py; checked again:
Contract of payments.py
  The output guarantees:
    unit_prices (unit): no two rows share id; "id" IS NOT NULL
  Each refresh checks on the data:
    unit_prices (unit): payments: cents ≥ 0; payments: no two rows share id; payments: "id" IS NOT NULL; payments: qty is NULL or (qty ≠ 0)

unit_prices (unit): proved
proved
exit code 0

data.text/markdown:
Now every refresh checks qty ≠ 0 on the data before it runs. The command has an exit code per outcome (3 for a refusal, 4 for a time budget, which SVERIFY_TIMEOUT sets), --format github annotates the pull request's lines, and --format sarif feeds code scanning (the command line).

2. A test for CI

A proof says the output meets the contract for every input that meets the preconditions. A test says the output is the one you meant on a few rows you chose. sverify.testing.assert_contract does both: it asserts the node's contract is proved, runs the node on your rows, checks both sides of the contract on them, and compares the output. Installing sverify registers it as a pytest plugin, so a test file in your suite needs only this:

assert_engines_agree(node, data) runs the same rows on every installed engine, and cases(node) draws inputs that meet the preconditions for Hypothesis (testing with pytest).

3. Credentials by name

A pipeline reads its lake with a token. The file names where the token lives, and sverify reads the value only when it opens a table: env:NAME for a variable, file: for a mounted secret, bao: for OpenBao, and each cloud's secret manager. A name in the project's pyproject.toml maps to one of those, so the file says "lake" and the deployment decides where it comes from. Reports, logs, errors and exports print the name:

node.credentials() lists the names a node uses before it runs, and sverify check warns when a sink lies outside what its credential may write (credentials).

4. Tell the next team what it gets

Finance's job reads your totals. It needs to know which version it read and what holds of it. OpenLineage is the standard for that: Airflow, Spark and dbt emit its events, and Marquez, DataHub and the cloud catalogs read them. A refresh with lineage= emits a run per node, with the columns each output column comes from and the node's contract. The payments are a Delta table with its change feed, and the node totals each merchant's payments:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
merchant_totals → totals:
  computed
  requires payments: max_rows(1000000000) (file stats @v0)
  requires payments: (_.cents >= 0) (file stats @v0)
  requires payments: (_.cents < 1000000000) (file stats @v0)
  route on duckdb: exact; evidence tested at 2.0.0 (facts duckdb-R6; #241)
  wrote totals from payments@v0: created v2, 1 row(s) written, 0 deleted

data.text/markdown: The events went to a file here; a URL sends them to Marquez or DataHub. The run's output carries the sverify_contract facet: each postcondition with its status, and the proved plan, exported to Substrait. Finance's pipeline reads the events and takes the postconditions as its requires, and sverify proves them again from the plan before it trusts them:

5. Late rows and bounded state

Finance also wants totals per hour. An hourly rollup keeps a row per merchant and hour, so its state grows with every hour it has seen. sv.arrives_within("ts", "PT1H") in requires says that no row arrives more than an hour behind the latest one. The refresh's retention line shows what it buys: the hours before the watermark are final, and the node drops them from its state, keeping them in the sink (Retention.expiry_sound):

console.name: stdout
console.text:
hourly:
  computed
  requires payments: arrives_within(ts, 1h) (no NULLs, latest 2026-11-03 03:40:00; each batch checked at refresh)
  requires payments: (_.ts >= datetime(2000, 1, 1)) (file stats @v0)
  requires payments: (_.ts < datetime(2100, 1, 1)) (file stats @v0)
  requires payments: (_.cents >= 0) (file stats @v0)
  requires payments: (_.cents < 1000000000) (file stats @v0)
  route on duckdb: exact; evidence tested at 2.0.0 (facts duckdb-R6; #241)
  wrote hourly from payments@v0: created v2, 4 row(s) written, 0 deleted
  retention hourly.hour: 2 bucket(s) open (bound 2), 2 retired, 2 state row(s); watermark 2026-11-03 02:40:00

data.text/markdown: The promise is checked on every batch. We'll append a payment from 00:05, which comes in after 03:40:

data.text/html: <marimo-callout-output data-html='"\u003cspan class=\"markdown prose dark:prose-invert contents\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"paragraph\"\u003ePreconditionError: 1 inserted row(s) of payments violate arrives_within(ts, 1h): ts before the watermark 2026-11-03 02:40:00 (the latest ts seen, 2026-11-03 03:40:00, minus 1h); the batch was rejected, nothing was applied\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e"' data-kind='"danger"'></marimo-callout-output>

data.text/markdown:
Nothing was applied: the closed hour finance reported on stays as it was, and the alert names the row, the watermark and the promise it broke. Whoever is on call decides whether the source or the promise is wrong, in the morning.

What you got

You can now check a pipeline's file in CI and let --fix write the preconditions a proof needs, test a node on rows you chose, keep credentials out of every file and log, hand the next team a contract it proves again, and bound a rollup's state with a promise every batch is checked against. That is the end of the tour. The guide covers every feature in more detail, and how it works goes under the hood: the checker, the producers and engines, and what is proved and what is trusted.
